title: Dots That Make an IP Address
statement:
Someone typed an IPv4 address and lost the dots. You get the digit string s. Return every valid IPv4 address you can make by inserting exactly three dots into s, without adding, removing or reordering digits.

A valid address has four parts. Each part is a number from 0 to 255, and a part may not have a leading zero: "0" is fine, "01" and "00" are not.

Return the addresses in any order. Return an empty list if there are none.

examples.why: "1.02.0.3" and "1.0.2.03" are rejected because "02" and "03" have leading zeros.
Each part is a single zero, which is allowed. "00" would not be.
"256" is too big, so the first part is "2" or "25". Every other split runs into "600" (too big) or a part like "011" or "00" (leading zero).

hints: Each part is 1 to 3 digits long. How many ways can you choose the lengths of four parts?
Build the address part by part. At each step try a part of length 1, 2 or 3 and check it before going deeper.
Prune early: stop if the part has a leading zero or exceeds 255, and stop if the digits left cannot fill the remaining parts (fewer than one or more than three digits per part).

explain.intuition:
An address is four parts of 1 to 3 digits each, so there are at most 3⁴ = 81 ways to choose part lengths. That makes this a small search, and backtracking is the natural shape: choose the first part, recurse on the rest of the string for the remaining three parts, and undo the choice to try the next length.

The rules that make a part valid are simple but easy to get wrong: at most 255, and no leading zero unless the part is exactly "0". Checking the leftover length early (it must fit between one and three digits per remaining part) cuts off hopeless branches, and lets you reject long strings immediately.
steps: Write go(start, parts) where parts holds the parts chosen so far.
If parts has four entries, record the address when start is at the end of s, then return.
Let left = 4 − parts.length. If the digits remaining are fewer than left or more than 3 · left, return.
For lengths 1 to 3, take the piece. Skip it if it has a leading zero (length > 1 and starts with 0) or is above 255. Otherwise push it, recurse, and pop it.
pitfalls: Allowing "0" but also "00" or "012". Only a lone zero may start with 0.
Comparing the part to 255 as a string: "99" > "255" in string order. Convert it to a number (or compare by length first).
Running past the end of the string when taking a 3-digit piece near the end, which silently creates shorter parts.

complexity.time: O(1): at most 81 length choices, each checked in constant time

solutions.title: Three nested cut positions
solutions.idea: Try every pair of three cut points directly, then validate the four pieces.

solutions.title: Backtracking with pruning
solutions.idea: Choose one part at a time (1 to 3 digits), validate it, recurse, and cut branches whose leftover length cannot fit.

followups: Do the same for IPv6-style groups of up to four hex digits. What changes in the pruning?
Only count the valid addresses for a string of length up to 10⁵ split into many parts. How would dynamic programming replace the search?
